1.e4 e5 2.Nf3.name: King's Knight Opening
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3.background: The most popular second move for White. It begins the Ruy Lopez, White's most frequent choice at the top level, the Italian Game, which has been analysed for hundreds of years, and the Scotch Game, which was popular in the nineteenth century.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nc6.strategy: The most natural reply: Black defends the attacked pawn and develops a piece in the same move, and the knight joins the fight for the centre. Black commits to nothing yet, and that is both the strength and the cost. Every set-up stays open, but White now decides what kind of game it becomes, from slow manoeuvring to sharp open play, and Black has to be at home in all of them.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nf6.strategy: Counterattacks e4 instead of defending e5, aiming for a solid, symmetrical position and sidestepping the main set-ups White would otherwise choose. Black must be careful, though: grabbing e4 at once after 3.Nxe5 is an error that leaves Black worse. The price is a drawish reputation and a large body of theory to learn.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d6.strategy: Defends e5 with a pawn and builds a compact, solid set-up, but a passive one: the f8-bishop is hemmed in and White usually gets more space with d4. Black must then choose between holding e5 and giving up the centre for piece play against e4. It is easy to understand and rarely seen at the top level.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Qe7.name: Gunderam Defence
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Qe7.background: Gerhart Gunderam first played it in a 1958 correspondence game against August Babel, but International Master Hélder Câmara had played it four years earlier, in 1954, in the Brazilian Championship. Brazilian players took it up, so that it came to be called the Brazilian Defence.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Qe7.strategy: Defends e5 with the queen, which blocks the f8-bishop and makes Black's development awkward. White develops freely with natural moves, while Black's plans of queenside castling or a later ...f5 cost time.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Qf6.name: Greco Defence
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Qf6.background: Named after Gioachino Greco, who gave a line against it in 1620. It is also called the McConnell Defence, and Paul Morphy met it against McConnell in New Orleans in 1849.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Qf6.strategy: Defends e5 but brings the queen out early and takes f6 from the knight on g8. White develops with tempo against the queen, for example with e5 or Nd5 later; the advantage is mainly one of smoother development.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Na6.strategy: Puts the knight on the rim, far from the centre, and ignores the attack on e5. After 3.Nxe5 White has won a pawn and can build the centre while the knight on a6 is misplaced.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Bd6.strategy: Defends e5 but blocks the d-pawn, and with it the c8-bishop, and invites 3.d4. After 3...exd4 4.Nxd4 White has the centre and a lead in development, and the bishop on d6 becomes a target for Nb5 and Nf5.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Bc5.name: Busch–Gass Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Bc5.background: The Busch–Gass Gambit was something of an online fad in the early 2020s.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Bc5.strategy: Develops with pressure on f2 and offers the e5-pawn. After 3.Nxe5 Nc6 4.Nf3 White is a pawn up with the knight safely back, and Black has only a small lead in development to show for it.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Bb4.strategy: Develops the bishop to a square where it pins nothing, since the white knight has not yet come to c3, and leaves e5 attacked. White takes the pawn with 3.Nxe5 and can gain time against the bishop with c3.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Nh6.strategy: Develops the knight to the rim, away from the centre, where Bxh6 can double Black's pawns once d3 or d4 has opened the c1-h6 diagonal. It also leaves e5 attacked, so 3.Nxe5 wins a pawn.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 a6.strategy: Guards b5 against a bishop that is not there yet and ignores the attack on e5. After 3.Nxe5 White has won a pawn, and if Black wins it back with ...Qe7 and ...Qxe4+, White still leads in development.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 a5.strategy: Spends a tempo on a rim pawn while e5 is attacked. 3.Nxe5 wins a pawn, and ...a5 contributes nothing to development or to the centre.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 b6.strategy: Prepares ...Bb7 against e4, but e5 is attacked and the bishop would not defend it. White takes the pawn with 3.Nxe5 and can answer ...Bb7 with d3.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 c6.name: King's Pawn Game: Gunderam Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 c6.strategy: Prepares ...d5 to challenge the e4-pawn, but does not defend e5. White takes the pawn with 3.Nxe5, and Black's challenge to e4 then costs further tempi.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 c5.name: Sicilian Defence: Jalalabad Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 c5.strategy: Does nothing for the attacked e5-pawn: the c-pawn move ignores the threat. After 3.Nxe5 d6 4.Nf3 White is simply a pawn up.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d5.name: Elephant Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d5.background: Also known as the Queen's Pawn Countergambit and the Turkish Gambit, it is considered unsound. Games cited for it include Lob–Eliskases (German correspondence, 1929), which White won, and Bondarevsky–Lilienthal (USSR, 1941) and Tal–Lutikov (Tallinn, 1964), which gave White the advantage.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d5.strategy: Strikes at e4 at the cost of a pawn: after 3.exd5 e4 4.Qe2 White keeps the extra pawn, and after 3.Nxe5 Black wins it back on e4 but White keeps the better game. Black can set traps but often ends up passive, with White holding the initiative and more space.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f5.strategy: Hits e4 at once and gives up the e-pawn after 3.Nxe5, aiming for open lines. The price is a loosened king, with the e8-h5 diagonal open to Qh5+, and with accurate play White keeps the better game.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 g6.strategy: Prepares ...Bg7 and a kingside fianchetto, but e5 remains attacked. After 3.Nxe5 White is a pawn up and can build a broad centre.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 h6.strategy: A waiting move that guards against Ng5 and Bg5 and does nothing about e5. 3.Nxe5 takes a pawn, and Black's only counter is ...Qe7 followed by ...Qxe4+, which still leaves White ahead in development.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 h5.strategy: Starts a kingside pawn advance without defending e5. After 3.Nxe5 White is a pawn up, and the h-pawn can no longer guard g5.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Qg5.strategy: Walks into 3.Nxg5: the knight on f3 attacks g5 and nothing protects the queen, so White wins it for nothing.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Qh4.strategy: Puts the queen on a square the knight on f3 attacks, so 3.Nxh4 wins it outright; nothing protects h4.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Ke7.strategy: Gives up castling for no reason, blocks the queen and the king's bishop, and leaves e5 attacked. After 3.Nxe5 White is a pawn up and Black's king stays in the centre.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Be7.strategy: Leaves e5 attacked and stands in the queen's way, so after 3.Nxe5 Black cannot hit back with ...Qe7 or ...Qf6. White is simply a pawn up.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Ba3.strategy: Throws the bishop away: 3.bxa3 takes it, and Black has no recapture and nothing in return.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Ne7.strategy: Blocks the queen and the king's bishop, does not defend e5, and takes away the ...Qe7 resource. 3.Nxe5 wins a pawn, and the knight on e7 is clumsily placed.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 b5.strategy: Gives a pawn away for nothing: 3.Bxb5 takes it, the bishop then pins the d7-pawn, and e5 is still attacked by the knight.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f6.name: Damiano Defence
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f6.background: Named after the Portuguese author Pedro Damiano, who in fact condemned the move as weak; in 1847 Staunton noted that it occurs in Damiano's old work. Chigorin played it against Schiffers at St Petersburg in 1897, and it is never seen in top-level play today.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f6.strategy: Defends e5 with a pawn but exposes the king and takes f6 from the knight. After 3.Nxe5 fxe5 4.Qh5+ Ke7 5.Qxe5+ White is clearly winning, and declining with 3...Qe7 still leaves Black worse.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 g5.strategy: Loosens the kingside while e5 hangs: 3.Nxe5 wins a pawn, and h4 then attacks the advanced g-pawn as well.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Bc5 3.Nxe5.strategy: Takes the pawn that Black's bishop move left unguarded. Black's compensation is only quick development and the bishop eyeing f2, which the king guards, so White is simply a pawn up and has to watch the tactics around f2 and f7.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Bc5 3.Bc4.strategy: Declines the pawn and develops with an eye on f7, but it gives Black time to defend e5 and reach an ordinary open game. White settles for equality instead of the extra pawn that the capture on e5 keeps.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Bc5 3.Nc3.strategy: Develops and guards the e4 pawn, leaving the e5 pawn for Black to look after. It is sound and keeps a normal open game, but White passes up the free pawn and the chance to punish the gambit.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Bc5 3.Nxe5 Nc6.name: King's Pawn Game: Busch-Gass Gambit, Chiodini Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Bc5 3.Nxe5 Nc6.strategy: Attacks the knight that took the pawn, but cannot win it back by force: White trades it off or retreats and stays a pawn up, while Black has only the active bishop to show for it.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Bc5 3.Nxe5 d6.strategy: Kicks the knight at once and opens the c8-bishop, accepting the lost pawn for a compact, sound position. The active bishop on c5 is the only compensation, so the game is a slow one in which White's extra pawn is the one real difference.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Bc5 3.Nxe5 Qh4.strategy: The gambit's point: the queen and bishop threaten mate on f2, and the queen eyes e4. White blocks the diagonal with a pawn move that also attacks the bishop; Black regains the pawn but falls far behind in development with the queen exposed. Blocking with g3?? loses at once to ...Qxe4+ and ...Qxh1.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d5 3.exd5.strategy: Accepts the gambit by taking the pawn that offers the centre, and keeps the extra pawn. Recapturing with the queen costs Black time, so Black must find compensation in activity, while White enjoys the more comfortable position.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d5 3.Nxe5.strategy: Takes the other pawn. Black can win the e4 pawn back, but the knight on e5 eyes f7 and White gets pressure on the kingside, so this capture also keeps an advantage. It is the less common of the two captures.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d5 3.d4.strategy: Strikes in the centre at once instead of taking a pawn. Black can open the position with ...dxe4 and White regains the pawn on e5, so the game becomes level and White gives up the extra pawn that either capture would keep.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d5 3.exd5 e4.name: Elephant Gambit: Paulsen Countergambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d5 3.exd5 e4.background: Named after Louis Paulsen, a nineteenth-century German master known for his deep opening ideas.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d5 3.exd5 e4.strategy: The main way to play the gambit: the pawn drives the knight from f3 and tries to seize the initiative with Black's space in the centre and rapid piece play. The knight is attacked, but White can hold the position with a pin on the e-pawn and keep the extra pawn, so Black must play accurately and still stands worse.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d5 3.exd5 Bd6.name: Elephant Gambit: Maróczy Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d5 3.exd5 Bd6.strategy: Develops the bishop, guarding e5 and preparing ...e4, instead of recapturing the pawn at once. White keeps the extra pawn and a clear advantage, though without an immediate attack.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d5 3.exd5 Nf6.strategy: Develops with an attack on the d5 pawn instead of recapturing with the queen. If White grabs the e5 pawn as well, Black wins one pawn back with the knight or queen but is still a pawn down, so the move asks for initiative rather than material.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d5 3.Nxe5 dxe4.strategy: Wins back the pawn at once, so material is level, and opens the centre and the d-file. The price is that f7 is now the target: the knight on e5 already eyes it, and a bishop arriving on c4 adds to the pressure while Black has not developed a single piece.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d5 3.Nxe5 Bd6.strategy: Challenges the intruding knight at once and develops while doing so, instead of rushing to win the pawn back. Black aims to trade off White's active knight and open the centre, but the pieces come off in the main line and White keeps a slightly better endgame with the bishop pair.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d5 3.Nxe5 Nf6.strategy: Develops with an attack on the e4 pawn and keeps the choice of recapture open. If White takes on d5, Black wins one pawn back but is still a pawn down, so Black plays for activity rather than material.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d5 3.Nxe5 dxe4 4.Bc4.strategy: Develops the bishop with a direct threat to f7, which the knight on e5 already attacks and only the king defends. Black has no easy way to hold the pawn and develop at the same time, so White gets overwhelming pressure on f7.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d5 3.Nxe5 dxe4 4.d4.strategy: Supports the knight on e5 with a central pawn and takes space, so Black cannot easily chase the knight away. The pawn on e4 stays a target and White keeps a lead in the centre, with the pressure on f7 still to come.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d5 3.Nxe5 dxe4 4.Nc3.strategy: Develops with a threat to win the e4 pawn, so Black must defend or counterattack at once. It leaves f7 alone, and the knight on e5 stands without support, which gives Black counterplay against it.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d5 3.Nxe5 dxe4 4.Bc4 Qg5.name: Elephant Gambit: Wasp Variation
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d5 3.Nxe5 dxe4 4.Bc4 Qg5.strategy: The most resilient reply: the queen hits the knight on e5 and the g2 pawn together, so White cannot take on f7 for nothing. After 5.Bxf7+ Ke7 6.d4 Black's king is exposed, yet ...Qxg2 regains the pawn and keeps the game sharp.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d5 3.Nxe5 dxe4 4.Bc4 Nf6.strategy: Develops and guards the e4 pawn but ignores f7: 5.Bxf7+ wins a pawn with check, and the king must go to e7 because the knight on e5 guards the bishop. White keeps the extra material while Black's king stands in the centre.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 d5 3.Nxe5 dxe4 4.Bc4 Be6.strategy: Shields f7 and offers a bishop trade, but 5.Bxe6 fxe6 wrecks Black's pawns and opens the f-file. After 6.Qh5+ g6 7.Nxg6 hxg6 8.Qxh8 Black has lost a rook for a knight, with no compensation.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f6 3.Nxe5.strategy: The refutation of 2...f6. The pawn on f6 only looks like a defender: it takes the best square from the king's knight and opens the e8-h5 diagonal, so White takes e5 and, if Black recaptures with the f-pawn, the queen comes out with check. White sacrifices a knight for a winning attack.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f6 3.Bc4.strategy: Develops the bishop where it already eyes the g8 knight across the empty diagonal. With the knight denied f6 and the king exposed on the e8-h5 diagonal, plain development is enough to leave Black struggling for a sound set-up.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f6 3.d4.strategy: Strikes at the centre at once while Black's king's knight lacks its natural square. If Black takes, the recapture comes with a lead in development and an open game, in which the weakened e8-h5 diagonal keeps hurting the king.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f6 3.Nxe5 Qe7.strategy: Declines the poisoned knight and attacks it instead, with the e4 pawn behind, so Black wins the pawn back; it also sets a trap for a White player who checks on h5 on autopilot. It only limits the damage: White keeps a lead in development and Black's f-pawn stays misplaced.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f6 3.Nxe5 fxe5.strategy: Wins a knight for a pawn on the board, but the e8-h5 diagonal is already open: the queen checks the king and attacks the pawn on e5 in one move, and Black cannot keep the extra piece. Every defence leaves White with a clear advantage.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f6 3.Nxe5 d5.strategy: Attacks the knight, but the e8-h5 diagonal is open: 4.Qh5+ g6 5.Nxg6 wins the rook on h8 whichever way Black recaptures or declines, and the king walk is no better.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f6 3.Nxe5 d6.strategy: Attacks the knight with a pawn but never recovers the pawn on e5, and 4.Qh5+ g6 5.Nxg6 wins the rook on h8 just the same. Black is a pawn down at best, with the kingside as weak as before.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f6 3.Nxe5 fxe5 4.Qh5+.strategy: The point of the sacrifice: the recapture leaves e5 loose, and the queen checks the king down the open e8-h5 diagonal while attacking that pawn along the fifth rank. Black cannot meet both threats without giving back far more than the knight.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f6 3.Nxe5 fxe5 4.d4.strategy: Opens the centre but wastes the one move the open diagonal allows: Black takes h5 away by developing the king's knight with a threat on e4, and White is a knight down for a pawn with nothing to show for it.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f6 3.Nxe5 fxe5 4.Bc4.strategy: Develops the bishop, but the sacrifice only works while the queen can use h5 and the e5 pawn is loose. Black takes h5 away by developing the king's knight, and White is simply a piece down for a pawn.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f6 3.Nxe5 fxe5 4.Qh5+ g6.strategy: Blocks the check with a pawn, but it leaves e5 hanging, and the queen's capture there checks the king while attacking the rook on h8. Black loses the exchange, which is still the lesser evil: walking the king instead loses more.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f6 3.Nxe5 fxe5 4.Qh5+ Ke7.strategy: Walks the king into the open instead of blocking. The queen takes on e5 with check, the king is driven to f7 and chased by the bishop, and White ends with several pawns for the knight against a king that can never castle. It loses more than the pawn block.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f6 3.Nxe5 fxe5 4.Qh5+ g6 5.strategy: A fork: the queen checks the king down the e-file and, across the empty f6 and g7 squares, attacks the rook on h8. Black must answer the check, so White wins the rook for the sacrificed knight and stays clearly better.
Takes a pawn with check, but the h7 pawn recaptures and White has given the queen for a pawn.
Saves the queen from the pawn but gives up the point of the sacrifice. Without the capture on e5 White is a knight down for a single pawn, and Black simply develops and keeps the piece.

Blocks the check and offers a queen trade, which White should decline: after the trade White would have only two pawns for the knight. Taking the rook instead wins the exchange, and Black at least regains the e4 pawn with check. The other ways out of check lose the rook too.
Steps aside and gives up castling. The queen takes the rook on h8 and Black has no check to gain time, while the exposed king still has the bishop's checks to fear.
Blocks with the bishop, but the queen takes the rook on h8 with no check for Black to gain time, and the knight on g8 is attacked as well. Black gets nothing for the exchange.
Blocks with the knight, but the queen takes the rook on h8 with no check for Black to gain time and then eyes the bishop on f8 and the h7 pawn. The rook is lost for nothing.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f6 3.Nxe5 fxe5 4.Qh5+ g6 5.name: King's Pawn Game: Damiano Defence, Damiano Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f6 3.Nxe5 fxe5 4.Qh5+ g6 5.strategy: Takes the rook rather than trading queens, which would leave White with two pawns for the knight. The queen on h8 also attacks the knight on g8, but Black's check on e4 gains time to save it. White is the exchange up and clearly better, though the queen is far from home.
Trades queens and throws away the point of the attack. The rook on h8 is safe after the recapture, and White is left with only two pawns for the knight.
Grabs a pawn but leaves the rook alone. Black takes e4 with check, keeps the rook, and White has only pawns for the knight with the queen far from home.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f6 3.Nxe5 Qe7 4.Nf3.strategy: Steps out of the attack and gives the pawn back, content with a lead in development against a queen out early and an f-pawn that blocks the king's knight. It also avoids the greedy check on h5, which would leave the queen and knight both attacked.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f6 3.Nxe5 Qe7 4.Qh5+.strategy: The reflex check from the 3...fxe5 line, but here there is no pawn on e5 to take. After ...g6 the queen is attacked by the pawn and the knight by pawn and queen, and White ends a piece down for a pawn.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f6 3.Nxe5 Qe7 4.Nc4.strategy: Keeps the knight but loses time. Black takes e4 with check, material is level, and the knight is soon hit again by ...d5, so White's lead in development shrinks.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f6 3.Nxe5 Qe7 4.Nf3 d5.name: King's Pawn Game: Damiano Defence, Damiano Gambit, Chigorin Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f6 3.Nxe5 Qe7 4.Nf3 d5.background: In a 1964 simultaneous exhibition Robert McGregor met Bobby Fischer with 4...d5 and drew, although Fischer did not play the best moves. Modern Chess Openings analyses 4...d5 5.d3 dxe4 6.dxe4, when White had a small advantage.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f6 3.Nxe5 Qe7 4.Nf3 d5.strategy: Instead of taking e4 with the queen at once, Black challenges the centre with a pawn, attacks e4 a second time and frees the c8-bishop. The pawn can still be won back, but White keeps a small advantage.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f6 3.Nxe5 Qe7 4.Nf3 Qxe4+.strategy: Takes the pawn back with check, so material is level. The queen is exposed in the centre and White gains time chasing it, while the pawn on f6 stays misplaced, blocking the king's knight. Black has to accept a deficit in development as the price.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 f6 3.Nxe5 Qe7 4.Nf3 Nc6.strategy: Develops a piece but leaves the pawn on e4 alone. White defends it with a developing move and stays a pawn up, with the better development as well.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Qe7 3.Bc4.strategy: Develops the bishop to its most active square, with an eye on f7, and takes advantage of the queen standing in the way of Black's own bishop. White gets a comfortable lead in development and a free hand in the centre.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Qe7 3.Nc3.strategy: Defends e4 with a developing move, so the centre is secure and the bishops are still free to choose their squares. White meets the odd queen move with normal development and lets Black prove that the set-up works.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Qe7 3.d3.strategy: A modest pawn move: e4 is guarded and the c1-bishop freed, but White does not use Black's awkward set-up, with the queen blocking its own bishop, to claim space or develop actively. Safe, but slow.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Qe7 3.Bc4 f5.name: King's Pawn Game: Gunderam Defence, Gunderam Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Qe7 3.Bc4 f5.background: Gerhart Gunderam suggested the ...f5 break after 2...Qe7 and analysed this sharp line; he published his analysis of the opening in his 1961 book Neue Eröffnungswege.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Qe7 3.Bc4 f5.strategy: Breaks in the centre at once, aiming to open the f-file and gain time after exf5. The price is a loosened king: f7 and g8 are open to White's bishop, and the queen still blocks the f8-bishop. Sharp and playable, but Black has to prove the compensation.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Qe7 3.Bc4 c6.strategy: A sound, flexible reply to the bishop's pressure on f7, which the king and queen hold. The pawn takes d5 under control and prepares to challenge the centre, in return for a slightly cramped set-up in which the queen still blocks the f8-bishop.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Qe7 3.Bc4 d6.strategy: Supports e5 with a pawn, which relieves the queen of that duty, and opens the c8-bishop. A modest, safe move; the cost is a passive pawn chain, and the f8-bishop stays shut in behind the queen for now.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Qf6 3.Bc4.strategy: A natural developing move that eyes f7 and makes use of the queen's awkward post: the knight is denied its best square, and White can aim for a lead in development.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Qf6 3.Nc3.strategy: Develops a piece and threatens Nd5 with tempo on the queen, so Black has to spend a move on a precaution while White keeps developing. The queen's early outing costs Black time, and White's lead grows without any risk.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Qf6 3.d4.strategy: Opens the centre at once to exploit the queen's early outing. If Black takes on d4, White regains the pawn with the knight and the open lines favour the better-developed side; but the break is less forcing than simple development, because Black has other ways to meet it.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Qf6 3.Bc4 Qg6.strategy: Attacks e4 and g2 at once, but it is a lure: castling covers g2, and ...Qxe4? runs into Bxf7+, which wins the queen or drives the king across the board. Black has moved the queen twice and developed nothing while White is ahead in development.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Qf6 3.Bc4 c6.strategy: The solid answer: the pawn prepares ...d5, which would hit both the bishop and the e4 pawn, and it covers d5 and b5 in the meantime. It spends a move on a pawn while White is ahead in development, but it takes away White's easy targets.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Qf6 3.Bc4 Nc6.strategy: Defends e5 with a developing move, so the queen is no longer tied to the pawn. It is the natural square for the knight, but White keeps the lead in development and can open the centre while Black's king is still in the middle.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Qf6 3.Bc4 h6.strategy: Takes the g5 square away from White's knight, so the attack on f7 cannot grow with Ng5. A quiet precaution that costs a tempo while White leads in development, but it removes the most direct threat.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Qf6 3.Bc4 Qg6 4.O-O.name: King's Pawn Game: La Bourdonnais Gambit
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Qf6 3.Bc4 Qg6 4.O-O.background: Named for La Bourdonnais, the gambit was also analysed by Greco.
1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Qf6 3.Bc4 Qg6 4.O-O.strategy: Castles to guard g2 with the king and leaves e4 as poisoned bait. If Black takes it, Bxf7+ is very strong: ...Kxf7?? loses the queen to Ng5+, and otherwise the king is chased across the board. White gets development for a pawn.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Qf6 3.Bc4 Qg6 4.Nc3.strategy: Defends e4 with a developing move rather than castling, and eyes d5. The g2 pawn stays loose, but ...Qxg2 is met by Rg1 hitting the queen, so Black takes a pawn at the price of falling further behind in development.

1.e4 e5 2.Nf3 Qf6 3.Bc4 Qg6 4.d3.strategy: Defends e4 with a pawn and opens the diagonal of the c1 bishop, but it is slower than castling and leaves g2 unguarded. Black can take it with ...Qxg2, and White must make the lead in development pay for the pawn.
